mil3.2.3:1.2: “Venerable Nāgasena, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, has wisdom arisen?”
mil3.2.3:1.3: “Yes, Great King, for one in whom knowledge has arisen, wisdom has arisen.”
mil3.2.3:1.5: “Yes, Great King, knowledge itself is wisdom.”
mil3.2.3:1.6: “But venerable sir, one in whom that very knowledge, that very wisdom, has arisen—would he be deluded, or would he not be deluded?”
mil3.2.3:1.7: “He might be deluded about some things, Great King, and not deluded about others.”
mil3.2.3:1.9: “He might be deluded, Great King, about branches of craft he has not known before, about a direction he has not gone to before, or about a designation of a name he has not heard before.”
mil3.2.3:1.11: “But whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’—about that, Great King, he would not be deluded.”
mil3.2.3:1.12: “But where does his delusion go, venerable sir?”
mil3.2.3:1.13: “As soon as knowledge arises, Great King, delusion ceases right there.”
mil3.2.3:2.2: “Suppose, Great King, a certain man were to bring a lamp into a dark house; then the darkness would cease and light would appear;
mil3.2.3:2.3: in the same way, Great King, as soon as knowledge arises, delusion ceases right there.”
mil3.2.3:3.2: “Wisdom too, Great King, having done its task, ceases right there; but whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’ does not cease.”
mil3.2.3:4.1: “Venerable Nāgasena, when you say ‘wisdom, having done its task, ceases right there, but whatever has been established by that wisdom as “impermanent”, “suffering”, or “not-self” does not cease’, give me a simile for that.”
mil3.2.3:4.2: “Suppose, Great King, a man who wanted to send a letter at night were to have a scribe summoned, have a lamp lit, and have the letter written. When the letter had been written he would have the lamp put out, but even though the lamp was put out, the letter would not be lost.
mil3.2.3:4.3: In the same way, Great King, wisdom, having done its task, ceases right there; but whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’ does not cease.”
mil3.2.3:5.2: “Suppose, Great King, in the eastern provinces people place five water pots at each house for putting out a blaze. When a house catches fire they throw those five water pots over the house, and the fire goes out. Great King, would those people think: ‘We will put those pots to use again’?”
mil3.2.3:5.3: “No, venerable sir. Enough of those pots! What use are those pots?”
mil3.2.3:5.4: “Great King, as the five water pots, so should the five faculties be seen: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of immersion, and the faculty of wisdom.
mil3.2.3:5.5: As those people, so should the practitioner be seen.
mil3.2.3:5.7: As the fire is put out by the five water pots, so the defilements are put out by the five faculties; and defilements that have been put out do not arise again.
mil3.2.3:5.8: In the same way, Great King, wisdom, having done its task, ceases right there; but whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’ does not cease.”
mil3.2.3:6.2: “Suppose, Great King, a physician were to take five root medicines, go up to a sick person, grind up those five root medicines and give them to the sick person to drink, and by them the disorders would be expelled. Great King, would that physician think: ‘I will use those five root medicines again for the work of medicine’?”
mil3.2.3:6.3: “No, venerable sir. Enough of those five root medicines! What use are those five root medicines?”
mil3.2.3:6.4: “Great King, as the five root medicines, so should the five faculties be seen: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of immersion, and the faculty of wisdom; as the physician, so should the practitioner be seen.
mil3.2.3:6.6: As the sick person, so should the ordinary person be seen.
mil3.2.3:6.7: As the sick person’s disorders are expelled by the five root medicines, and when the disorders have been expelled the sick person is healthy, so the defilements are expelled by the five faculties; and defilements that have been expelled do not arise again.
mil3.2.3:6.8: In the same way, Great King, wisdom, having done its task, ceases right there; but whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’ does not cease.”
mil3.2.3:7.2: “Suppose, Great King, a warrior who fights in battle were to take five arrows and go down into battle to defeat the enemy army. Having gone into the battle, he would shoot those five arrows, and by them the enemy army would be broken. Great King, would that warrior who fights in battle think: ‘I will use those arrows again for the work of arrows’?”
mil3.2.3:7.3: “No, venerable sir. Enough of those arrows! What use are those arrows?”
mil3.2.3:7.4: “Great King, as the five arrows, so should the five faculties be seen: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of immersion, and the faculty of wisdom.
mil3.2.3:7.5: As the warrior who fights in battle, Great King, so should the practitioner be seen.
mil3.2.3:7.7: As the enemy army is broken by the five arrows, so the defilements are broken by the five faculties; and defilements that have been broken do not arise again.
mil3.2.3:7.8: In the same way, Great King, wisdom, having done its task, ceases right there; but whatever has been established by that wisdom as ‘impermanent’, ‘suffering’, or ‘not-self’ does not cease.”
